faq.a: A solstice is when one of Earth's poles leans most towards the Sun, giving the longest day in one hemisphere and the shortest in the other. Solstices fall around 21 June and 21 December.
An equinox is when Earth's tilt is side-on to the Sun, so the Sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are nearly equal everywhere. Equinoxes fall around 20 March and 22 September.

faq.q: Why do the dates of solstices change a little?
faq.a: A year is about 365 and a quarter days, not exactly 365, so solstices and equinoxes shift about six hours later each year, then jump back when a leap day is added.
asks: Is the solstice always on the 21st?

faq.q: Why does Stonehenge line up with the Sun?
faq.a: Its builders, about 4,500 years ago, arranged the great stones so that the midsummer Sun rises along its main line and the midwinter Sun sets along it. It may have helped them mark the turning of the year.
asks: What does Stonehenge have to do with the solstice?

faq.q: Is the June solstice the hottest day?
faq.a: Usually not. Land and sea keep warming for weeks after the solstice, so the hottest weather often comes in July or August, a delay called seasonal lag.
asks: Why is July hotter than June?

facts: The word solstice comes from Latin words meaning sun and standing still.
Equinox comes from the Latin for equal night.
Stonehenge's main axis lines up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.

quiz.why: At an equinox Earth's tilt is side-on to the Sun, so every place gets about 12 hours of daylight.
